subject: Making awkward kitchen spaces useful
hook: Out-of-square walls, a boxed-in pipe and an odd corner: how an awkward kitchen gets planned properly.
ig:
Out-of-square walls, a boxed-in pipe and an odd corner: how an awkward kitchen gets planned properly.

The secret to using every bit of an awkward kitchen isn't a clever product. It's a thorough survey.

Here's the typical sequence:

1. Measure walls at more than one height, because they're rarely the same top to bottom.
2. Mark every pipe, boiler, socket and recess on the sketch.
3. Plan in 3D so you can see the corners and pull-outs in place.
4. Make units to the widths the room needs, not the nearest catalogue size.
5. Scribe filler panels on site to follow the walls.
6. Check that services are still accessible behind removable panels.

Skip step 1 or 2 and the awkward bits get covered up instead of used.

Save this so you know what a good kitchen survey should include, whoever you choose to build it.
fb:
Awkward kitchens aren't solved on fitting day. They're solved at the survey.

When we measure a kitchen, we're checking walls at different heights, marking every pipe and boiler, and noting each recess. That's what lets us design units to the exact widths the room needs, then scribe them to the walls when our team fits them.

This carousel walks through the typical sequence. If you'd like to see finished pieces from our workshop, take a look at our showcase:
